title: Keepers of the Holy Land
hook: brown-robed friars who keep watch over the places of Jesus's life, and the walk they brought home

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Franciscan crown, a rosary that walks through Mary's joys. Your line was seven joys.

A brown habit. A rope belt with knots in it. Sandals. That outfit belongs to Assisi, to Francis and his brothers. But you can also meet it in the stone streets of Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Nazareth, on a friar who isn't visiting. He lives there. He sweeps a shrine, unlocks a door for pilgrims at dawn, and sings the hours in a chapel built over a place from the Gospels. Tradition says the brothers of Francis have kept watch over these places for centuries. Today, those keepers, and the walk they carried home.
screen: `A BROWN HABIT, A ROPE BELT.` → `IN JERUSALEM, NOT ASSISI.` → `HE ISN'T VISITING. HE LIVES THERE.`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred fifty, you met the Stations; today, the friars behind them. They call their charge the Custody of the Holy Land, and the brother who leads them is the Custos, the keeper. The job is plain and endless: care for the shrines, pray in them, and welcome pilgrims with sore feet. Some of the holiest places aren't theirs alone. The church over Calvary and the empty tomb is shared by several Christian churches, Orthodox and Armenian and others alongside the Catholics, each with its own corners and hours. So keeping the Holy Land means keeping the peace in it. Then there's the walk. In Jerusalem, pilgrims wanted to follow the road Jesus took to the cross, stopping to pray. Luke tells one of those stops. Women follow him, weeping, and he turns to them. In the Douay-Rheims: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children." But not everyone can get to that street. So the walk was carried home. The friars helped spread the Stations of the Cross, crosses or pictures on a church wall, so a grandmother in a village could walk the road to Calvary in her own parish. A surprise on that wall: some stops come straight from the Gospels, like Simon of Cyrene taking up the cross, and some from tradition, like Veronica wiping his face. The Gospels never mention her. The Stations hold both, and the friars kept both.
screen: `THE CUSTODY: KEEP, PRAY, WELCOME.` · `HOLY PLACES SHARED WITH OTHER CHURCHES.` · `A WALK THROUGH JERUSALEM'S STREETS.` · `THE WALK CARRIED HOME TO EVERY PARISH.` · then, large: `DAUGHTERS OF JERUSALEM, WEEP NOT OVER ME.`

segments.voice: Stand if you can, take a few slow steps and stop, and bring to mind Jesus handed over to die; a few more steps, and Simon, a stranger pulled from the crowd to carry the cross; a few more, and the women on the road, and the words he said to them. If you pray, say an Our Father at the last stop; if not, just stand still and let the road be quiet.
Keepers of the Holy Land. The friars in brown who care for the places of Jesus's life, and who helped carry his road home to every parish. Today's word.
screen: `KEEPERS OF THE HOLY LAND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the custody. Some keep watch in Jerusalem, and the road comes home to every parish wall. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross in parish churches, especially on the Fridays of Lent, walking or turning from one station to the next; in Jerusalem, Franciscan friars lead the walk through the streets of the old city.

options: give up: it only counts in Jerusalem.
send someone else to walk it for you.

fork.reveal: that's what the Stations are for. the friars helped carry Jerusalem's walk home, so anyone could take it in their own church.

chat.says: Why do Catholic churches have those Stations of the Cross pictures on the walls?
options: So people far from Jerusalem can walk Jesus's road to the cross in their own parish.
They mark the fourteen places where Jesus taught his disciples in the Temple.
They are pictures of the martyrs of Jerusalem who died guarding the holy places.
chat.meaning: Pilgrims walked Jesus's road in Jerusalem; the friars helped carry that walk home as the Stations, so anyone could take it in their parish.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's date (1342, the papal recognition of the Franciscan custody under Clement VI) is left out of the voice; the voice says only 'tradition says ... for centuries'. Confirm that phrasing.
Confirm: the head of the Custody is called the Custos; friars of the Custody serve shrines in Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Nazareth.

Confirm the fair description of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre as shared by several churches (Greek Orthodox, Armenian Apostolic, Catholic via the Franciscans, with Coptic, Ethiopian and Syriac presences) without counts.

The Franciscan role in spreading the Stations is taken from the index hook (e.g., St. Leonard of Port Maurice in the 18th century; the indulgence attached to Stations erected by Franciscans). Stated generally; confirm.
Veronica and Jesus's falls are not in the canonical Gospels; Simon of Cyrene (Luke 23:26) and the women of Jerusalem (Luke 23:27–31) are. Confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 23:28 to confirm.
